catalog_quote: Stress in words of more than one syllable lies as a rule on the syllabic preceding the last consonant of the word, e.g., 'joku, "dog"; 'mijɛ, "woman"; ho'kolo, "young"; ... but: fa'ləm, "head"; ... a'waw, "mother's brother"; ... holo'boj, "carrying net"; ... In words of 3 and 4 syllables, ending in a vowel, which have the antepenult closed by a consonant, the stress tends to shift to this syllable, if the penult is an open syllable in ə, e.g., 'wəwnəle, "thou wilt say to him"; ... but: how'boke, "he killed (something)" ... In longer words the main stress falls on the regular syllabic according to the basic rule stated above, a secondary stress affecting the 3rd syllable forward from the main stress, or the 2nd syllable forward if this is closed by a consonant, e.g., ha,bəwdo'koke, "he hit me" (aor.); ...,ədəka'wale, "I saw thee"; ... [p.10] Deviations and variations from the above rule…
sweep_summary: Three works with stress in the title, all Elenbaas: the 1999 Utrecht/LOT dissertation (already held by the project, open access, image-only scan with scanned of the stress chapter), the 1996 Linguistics in the Netherlands paper 'Ternary rhythm in Sentani' (downloaded today as an open-access PDF from jbe-platform, DOI 10.1075/avt.13.08ele, saved with text), and Glottolog 674547, which is a duplicate record of the 1996 paper with the volume editors Cremers and den Dikken in the author slot. Both Elenbaas texts state the same first-hand rule from 1994 fieldwork: main stress on the penult when the final syllable is light, on the final syllable when it is heavy (closed by a nasal, or a diphthong), with 'all words ending in heavy syllables are stressed in my data' (1999, print p.58); secondary stress on the 2nd/even syllables, or the 1st if heavy or if the 2nd is an open schwa syllable, with clash avoidance producing ternary intervals. This refines the catalog's weight-hedged coding from Cowan 1965: the weight-sensitive penult/final rule is confirmed by an independent dedicated stress study (and by Hartzler 1976, Central dialect, held by the project), and Cowan's 'tends to shift' to a closed antepenult corresponds to Elenbaas's secondary stress, not to variable main stress. Best new statement: Elenbaas 1999 sec. 3.5.1, which should supersede Cowan as the deciding source (with the 1996 paper p.61 as a second locator). Nothing left unread among the items; no remained, but no further title needed searching.

new_statements.quote: If the final syllable is light, main stress falls on the penultimate syllable. [...] If the final syllable is heavy, main stress will fall on this final syllable. Closed syllables and diphthongs are heavy, open syllables are light. As already mentioned in the section 3.3, only nasals can fill coda positions and only diphthongs may form a branching nucleus. Only a few word-final suffixes end in a nasal or a diphthong. Inflected verbs mostly end in CV, as a result of which final heavy syllables are relatively rare. Nevertheless, all words ending in heavy syllables are stressed in my data.

new_statements.reading: Quantity-sensitive right-edge main stress: penultimate syllable unless the final syllable is heavy (nasal-closed or diphthong), in which case final; stated as exceptionless in a first-hand corpus (1994 fieldwork, 4 Central + 2 Eastern speakers, transcriptions cross-checked by four other phonologists). This is the same rule Cowan 1965 expresses as 'the syllabic preceding the last consonant' (his a'waw, holo'boj = final diphthongs), and the same as Hartzler 1976 (Central dialect, p.67, held by the project: penult if word ends in an open syllable, final if closed or laryngealized). Cowan's hedge about stress 'tending to shift' to a closed antepenult in 3-4 syllable words is reinterpreted by Elenbaas as secondary stress on a heavy initial/closed syllable (her 3.5.2), not variable main stress; she reports no lexically exceptional main stress. So the catalog's weight-sensitive coding is confirmed and its hedge can be dropped for main stress.

audit.recode_to: weight-sensitive (un-hedged): primary stress final if heavy (nasal-closed or diphthong/Vj,Vw), else penult; right edge, CVC(+VG) heavy. Drop the 'hedged' qualifier: Elenbaas 1999:58 ('all words ending in heavy syllables are stressed in my data') and Hartzler 1976:67 state the rule categorically; Cowan's 'as a rule'/'tends to' hedges concern lexical exceptions (p.10) and the schwa-penult antepenult shift, which Elenbaas's Central-dialect data do not show for main stress (50b [wə̀nnə́le] vs Cowan 'wəwnəle). Secondary-stress rule (the secondary-stress rule) should be re-read from Elenbaas 3.5.2: left-edge binary alternation (2nd syllable, or 1st if heavy / if 2nd is open-ə), quantity-sensitive, max lapse of two, rather than Cowan's '3rd syllable forward from the main stress'. Add Elenbaas 1999 and Hartzler 1976 to sources.

sources.note: Rule as stated: main stress on the syllable preceding the last consonant of the word, i.e. final syllable when the word ends in a consonant (only nasals and semivowels j, w may close a syllable, p. 9: 'nasal and semivowel being the only consonants admitted as syllable finals'), otherwise the penult; in 3-4 syllable vowel-final words a closed antepenult takes the stress if the penult is an open ə syllable (implicit weight scale closed > open full vowel > open ə). Secondary stress: 3rd syllable before the main stress, or the 2nd if it is closed (marked by a low dash). Domain: the word. Exception

sources.note: The only study devoted to Sentani stress, with the author's own 1994 fieldwork (6 speakers, Central + Eastern dialects, independent transcribers); our record rested on Cowan 1965's two hedged paragraphs. downloaded: confirms final-if-heavy-else-penult without hedge and replaces Cowan's count-back secondary-stress rule with a left-edge quantity-sensitive alternating rule.

sources.quote: 'The phonological word (PW) is established as the domain of a single stress peak. The placement of this peak is predictable by the following general rules: (1) a. Stress occurs on the penultimate syllable when the word ends in an open syllable; b. Stress occurs on the ultimate syllable when the word ends in a closed or laryngealized syllable.' Adds (p.69-70) that stress alternation limits the PW to two or three syllables, longer strings being repetitions of the basic pattern; no secondary-stress rule stated.

sources.citation: Hyde, Brett & Paramore, Jonathan Charles. 2026. The Sentani variation. Phonology 43(e5): 1-23. doi:10.1017/S0952675726100293
sources.quote: Sentani places primary stress on the penult. In forms with four or fewer syllables, as in (1a)-(1c), Sentani places secondary stresses on every even-numbered syllable from the left preceding the penult. The result in four-syllable forms, as in (1c), is a clash involving the stresses on the penultimate and antepenultimate syllables. In forms with more than four syllables, as in (1d)-(1f), Sentani places secondary stress on every even-numbered syllable from the left preceding the penult except the antepenult. [...] Final heavy syllables always receive the primary stress, and initial heavy syllables always receive at least a secondary stress.

tone.summary: No tone content; word stress only (default penultimate primary stress with binary secondary rhythm, clash/lapse alternation, edge-limited weight sensitivity), data from Elenbaas 1999.

sources.citation: Koser, Nate. 2022. The atomic properties of stress. Phonology 39(2): 213-249. doi:10.1017/S0952675723000076
sources.quote: In Sentani, the final syllable is stressed if it is heavy, as in (39a) and (39d). Otherwise, the penult is stressed instead, as in the other examples in (39). Ternary iteration proceeds leftwards from the stressed penultimate or final syllable, as in (39c) and (39d). Iteration is interrupted by heavy syllables, which receive stress as in (39e) and (39f), unless this would create a clash, as in (39g) and (39h).

sources.citation: Lamont, Andrew. 2022. A restrictive, parsimonious theory of footing in directional Harmonic Serialism. Phonology 39(1): 41-78. doi:10.1017/S0952675722000082
sources.quote: [p. 64] Sentani exhibits bidirectional inexhaustive footing, as the words in (48) illustrate. Other than the trochaic head foot, feet are iambic. Because the head foot surfaces at the right edge of words, its headedness reflects a ban on stressed final syllables, which requires a variant of NonFinality [...] The other aspect of Sentani that requires an additional constraint is underparsing in six-syllable words (48e). [...] [p. 65] tetrasyllabic words surface with stress clash (48c), but longer even-parity words do not (48e).

sources.quote: Sentani is a Papuan language, spoken in Irian Jaya, the easternmost province of Indonesia (Elenbaas 1996, 1999). The rhythmic patterns of words of two to seven light syllables are exemplified below. [...] Main stress always falls on the penult, with a secondary stress on the second syllable in words of minimally four syllables, and another secondary stress on the fourth syllable in words of seven or more syllables. [...] Elenbaas argues that Sentani has an iambic stress system in which stress on final syllables is avoided.

sources.citation: Elenbaas, Nine. 1996. Ternary rhythm in Sentani. In Cremers & den Dikken (eds.), Linguistics in the Netherlands 1996 (AVT Publications 13:1), 61-72. Amsterdam/Philadelphia: John Benjamins.
sources.quote: In Sentani main stress falls on the penultimate syllable, when the final syllable is light and on the final syllable when this syllable is heavy. Closed syllables and diphthongs are heavy, open syllables are light. [p.62:] Secondary stress falls two or three syllables to the left of main stress or to the left of another secondary stress. [...] Heavy syllables receive stress. [...] Clashes of two adjacent stresses are avoided. [...] there is a preference to avoid stress on an open syllables ending in schwa, wherever this is possible.
sources.locator: sec. 1.1 'Stress patterns', p.61; secondary stress and observations (2)-(8), p.62; footnote 1 on data sources, p.61
sources.note: Same main-stress rule as the 1999 dissertation (penult if final light, final if final heavy; closed syllables and diphthongs heavy), plus secondary stress 2-3 syllables to the left, heavy syllables stressed unless clash, schwa avoidance, no lapses of 3+ unstressed syllables; OT analysis with binary iambs and *LAPSE. Footnote 1: analysis 'based partly on data given in Cowan (1965) and M. Hartzler (1976), but mostly.. on data collected by the author during fieldwork in Irian Jaya in the fall of 1994'.
